en: Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying by the banks of the Bahudā River between a pair of *śāla* trees, having just completed the conversion of Subhadra.
He was accompanied by great bodhisattvas, śrāvaka disciples, and the great Brahma kings.
The devas, nāgas, spirits, and various kings,
along with the entire great assembly, remained solemn and did not disperse.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly.
The Great Parinirvāṇa has now been fully expounded.
Previously, I have already described for you, Pu Guang Bodhisattva, the buddha-fields of the ten directions.
If any among this great assembly have doubts, you may quickly ask about them.
"The unsurpassed Dharma-treasure will soon perish.
When the great assembly heard these words of the Buddha,
they wept with such grief and choked sobs that they could not restrain themselves.
Only those who have realized liberation are unable to give rise to sorrowful attachment.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Nityadāna (Constant Giving) who,
empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, rose from his seat.
Joining his palms toward the Buddha, he spoke these words:
"I wish to ask a question, yet I fear it may offend the Holy One's mind.
I only pray that the Tathāgata will not take this as an offense."
The Buddha told Changshi:
"The Tathāgata has already transcended the eight worldly dharmas;
why then should you have any doubt?"
The Bodhisattva Changshi addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, after the Tathāgata has passed into extinction,
all sentient beings will no longer behold the physical body (rūpakāya) of the Tathāgata."
They shall not hear the true Dharma.
In the future age of the Semblance Dharma,
wholesome dharmas will gradually decline while evil increasingly blazes forth.
"At that time, what kind of meritorious deed should one teach sentient beings to perform so that it is most preeminent?
Then the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Constantly Bestowing:
Excellent, excellent!
The sentient beings of future ages are truly to be pitied. Why is this?
All sentient beings practice with diligent effort yet do not realize the true principle;
though they accumulate merit extensively, the retribution they obtain is extremely slight. Good son!
In future ages, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, kings, ministers, elders, householders, brahmins, and others will despise my Dharma;
they will treat the Triple Gem with scant respect, and there will be no reality in it.
Although they perform various good deeds, they do so seeking fame, seeking profit, or seeking to surpass others;
therefore, not for a single moment do they give rise to the mind of world-transcendence. Good son!
In the future age, during the period of the Semblance Dharma (śāsanapratirūpaka),
what are the immeasurable calamities and evil events?
All monastics and laypeople will fail to recognize the proper rules of the Dharma.
A donor organized a religious assembly and invited the monks,
yet he dispatched guards to station at the gates and doors to block the bhikṣus and prevent them from entering the assembly.
If poor beggars wish to enter to seek alms,
yet they are again obstructed and not permitted,
then such a gathering will merely waste food and drink, yielding no merit whatsoever.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who are solely intent on their own solitary goodness and do not transform others.
Seeing others perform virtuous deeds, they are unable to rejoice in them or assist them to any degree.
Such people as these possess but meager and inferior merit.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who, upon seeing the old temples, stupas, shrines, images, and scriptures of others falling into ruin and decay,
refuse to repair them, and instead speak as follows:
"This was not created by my ancestors;
what use is there in repairing it?
I would rather create a new one myself."
Good son, for all sentient beings, establishing new [meritorious works] is not as good as cultivating those that are old;
the latter brings far greater merit.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who, seeing others gathering to perform various meritorious deeds, [join them].
Seeking only fame and reputation,
they exhaust their family’s wealth and possessions for the sake of giving,
yet when they encounter the poor, the destitute, and the solitary, [they treat them with contempt].
Scolding and driving them out without providing even a hair’s breadth of aid—
such sentient beings are said to perform good deeds in a perverted manner;
practicing merit while deluded and insane is called performing merit in an improper way.
Such people as these are truly to be pitied;
they expend vast wealth yet obtain but meager merit.
"Good son,
at one time I addressed the great assembly:
'If a person were to provide offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions, as well as to the bodhisattvas and the community of śrāvakas, throughout incalculable (asaṃkhyeya) lifetimes;'"
It is not as good as someone giving a single mouthful of food and drink to an animal;
its merit surpasses the former by hundreds of thousands of millions of times, being immeasurable and boundless.
"Good son,

in various sūtras I have taught the practice of giving in order to cause those who have left the home life and those who remain at home to cultivate a mind of loving-kindness and compassion, and to give to the poor, the orphaned, the elderly, and even to hungry dogs."
My disciples do not understand my intention;
they devote themselves exclusively to making offerings to the Field of Reverence and fail to make offerings to the Field of Compassion.
The Field of Reverence refers precisely to the Triple Gem: the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
The field of compassion consists of the poor, the orphaned, the elderly, and even down to ants;
between these two types of fields,
the field of compassion is the most supreme.
"Good son, if there is another person who,
possessing abundant wealth and property, practices giving alone."
From birth until old age,
it is not as if there were another multitude of people who did not differ in terms of poverty, wealth, nobility, or lowliness.
Whether they be monastics or laypeople,
they should together exhort one another to each contribute a small amount of wealth to gather in one place,
and then provide appropriate alms to the poor, the orphaned, the elderly, those with malignant diseases, those suffering from grave illnesses, and those in distress.
The merit thereof is exceedingly great.
Even if one does not practice giving,
the power of giving generated within every thought-moment constantly arises without end.
Giving alone brings very little merit.
Son of good family,
in future ages, my disciples—
They delight in fine clothing and crave exquisite flavors;
they greedily seek profit and hoard wealth with stinginess;
they do not cultivate a mind of loving-kindness.
They habitually act with malice and anger;
when they see others performing wholesome deeds, they dispute and revile them together,
all saying:
This person maintains a wrong livelihood through flattery and crookedness in seeking fame and profit.
If they see a poor beggar receiving alms,
they further give rise to anger and think as follows:
For one who has left the household life, what use is there for giving?
One should simply cultivate the practices of meditative concentration and wisdom.
What use is there for agitating oneself with useless worldly affairs?
Those who harbor such thoughts are the retinue of Māra.
When their lives end, they will fall into the great hells and undergo suffering for a long time.
Emerging from the hells, they will fall among the hungry ghosts and experience great torment.
Emerging from the realm of hungry ghosts, five hundred lifetimes were spent falling among dogs.
Having emerged from the state of dogs, for five hundred successive births he was constantly born into poverty and lowliness,
perpetually afflicted by the various sufferings of hunger and destitution.
There is not a single moment of mental satisfaction. Why is this?
Because when seeing others give, one does not rejoice in it.
"Good son,
I recall that my attainment of Buddhahood was entirely due to practicing *dāna* (generosity) throughout vast eons to provide relief for sentient beings who were poor and in distress.
The Buddhas of the ten directions likewise attained Buddhahood through the practice of giving."
Therefore, in various sūtras I have said that all six pāramitās take giving as their primary foundation,
O son of good family.
For example, it is like a person whose two feet are both broken;
though they intend to walk a long distance, they are unable to go.
So it is with the bhikṣu.
"Even if one practices the five pāramitās for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges,
if one does not practice giving, one cannot reach the further shore of nirvāṇa,
O son of good family."
One who does not practice giving has impure precepts;
because the precepts are impure, there is no compassionate heart;
and one who lacks compassion and mercy is unable to endure.
Because there is no patience, there is no vigor;
because there is no vigor, there is no meditative concentration;
because there is no meditative concentration, there is no wisdom.
Because they lack wisdom, they are constantly susceptible to the influence of immeasurable adventitious afflictions. Good son,
this is the dharma-gate of giving.
It is that which all Buddhas of the three periods of time collectively revere and honor.
For this reason, among the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), the attraction through material gifts (*āmiṣadāna*) is the most excellent. Good son!
At one time I praised the observance of precepts;
at another time I praised patience;
and yet at another time I praised meditative concentration.
At one time he may praise wisdom;
at another time he may praise the dhūta ascetic practices;
and at yet another time he may praise having few desires.
At one time he may praise the śrāvakas,
and at another time he may praise the bodhisattvas;
thus, in various ways, he acts according to the different capacities of beings.
In future ages, various wicked bhikṣus, failing to understand my intention, will each cling to their own views and mutually condemn one another, thereby destroying my Dharma.
These wicked bhikṣus will likewise sit in the assembly and expound the sutras and the Dharma.
They do not grasp my profound intent;
by taking the literal meaning according to the words, they contravene the true reality of the unsurpassed, authentic Dharma.
They constantly say to themselves: "The meaning I have explained must accord with the Buddha's intention."
Other Dharma masters deceive both monastics and laypeople;
those who speak such words shall sink forever into the sea of suffering.
When various evil bhikṣus see others practicing meditative concentration, they further say these things:
This person is as ignorant as a stump;
they do not perceive what is practiced within the sutras and treatises.
One who speaks such words shall incur calamity and guilt for many kalpas.
Various wicked bhikṣus, for the sake of fame and profit, will mutually revile one another.
Some of these wicked bhikṣus may cultivate merit without relying on the sūtras and śāstras;
following their own personal views, they will take what is wrong to be right.
Unable to distinguish what is heterodox and what is orthodox, he addressed both monastics and laypeople everywhere, saying:
"I am able to know this; I am able to see this."
It should be known that such a person will swiftly cause my Dharma to perish.
Even those evil bhikṣus who uphold the Vinaya,
failing to comprehend the profound meaning within the Vinaya Piṭaka, shall speak as follows:
In the Vinaya Piṭaka, the Buddha permitted the eating of meat.
Good son, if I were to explain the meaning of eating meat, [it would be as follows].
It is that which causes confusion and distress for śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas of the lower stages.
Because ordinary bhikṣus slander it upon hearing it,
the fact that the Vinaya-piṭaka permits the eating of meat is entirely inconceivable.
"Good son,
from the time I first attained the Way until this very day,
there have been disciples who, in various places, accepted the eating of meat."
Ordinary people truly see them eating meat.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who see various bhikṣus manifesting the act of eating meat.
Still further, there are sentient beings who know that when the bhikṣus eat meat, they have deeply entered immeasurable gates of remedial practice.
Immeasurable bhikṣus severed the higher afflictions;
immeasurable bhikṣus severed the middle afflictions;
immeasurable bhikṣus severed the lower afflictions.
Immeasurable bhikṣus have been delivered and led into the Buddha-way.
The Tathāgata’s teaching and transformation are inconceivable.
Since my attainment of Buddhahood, I have—
My disciples have never eaten the flesh of living beings.
When I permitted the eating of meat within the Vinaya,
it was with the definite knowledge that such meat does not arise from the four great elements.
They are not born from a womb;
they are not born from an egg;
they are not born from moisture.
It is not born through transformation;
it does not unite with consciousness,
nor does it unite with life-force.
"You should know that such meat does not exist at all in the world. Good son,
in future ages there will be many evil bhikṣus."
In every place where they preach the sūtras and vinaya,
they grasp the meaning according to the literal text,
unaware of the Tathāgata’s concealed and secret intentions.
Good son, it is impossible for the Buddha,
having appeared in the world, to allow his disciples to eat the flesh of sentient beings.
"If one eats meat, how can they be called one of great compassion? Good son,
today within this assembly, countless beings each see things differently."
Some see the Tathāgata entering parinirvāṇa;
some see the Tathāgata remaining in the world for one kalpa;
and some see the Tathāgata remaining for immeasurable kalpas.
Some see the Tathāgata’s body as sixteen feet tall;
some see it as a small body;
others see it as a large body.

In some instances, one sees the Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya) seated within the Lotus Treasury World-Ocean, expounding the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground for the thousands of billions of Śākyamuni Buddhas;
in other instances, one sees the Dharma Body (dharmakāya) as identical to space—without discrimination, without marks, and unobstructed, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
In some cases, one sees this place as a forest of śāla trees consisting entirely of earth, sand, grass, wood, and rocky walls;
in other cases, one sees this place as purely adorned with gold, silver, and the seven treasures.
Or they may see this place as the locus where all Buddhas of the three periods of time have practiced;
or they may see this place as the inconceivable realm of the Buddhas, the true reality of the Dharma-body.
Good son, when the Buddhas appear in the world, whether traveling, staying, or residing,
all their actions are entirely free from worldly characteristics.
Furthermore, it does not depart from the worldly manifestation of the Dharma of the true mark.
What the Tathāgata has spoken contains all phenomena in their entirety;
it is expounded through the utterance of a single character, a single phrase, or a single sound.
The inconceivable unique quality of the Tathāgata is that he enables all sentient beings, according to their various kinds and diverse faculties and natures,
each to attain different understandings and distinct realizations.
This is not something known by the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas;
rather, through the power of his sovereign mastery,
the Tathāgata manifests or conceals himself according to the capacities of beings to teach and transform them.
In the age of the Semblance Dharma, various wicked bhikṣus do not understand my intention;
they cling to their own views and proclaim the twelve divisions of the sūtras,
taking the literal meaning according to the text and making definitive assertions.
"You should know that this person is an enemy to the Buddhas of the three periods of time;
they will swiftly cause my Dharma to perish. Good son."
The Buddhas always rely upon the two truths when teaching the Dharma.
When they teach the dharmas of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), they do not contradict the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
By using proximate meanings, they point toward the remote.
The standing image represents the profound mystery.
Various wicked bhikṣus, unable to comprehend this meaning within it,
slander and do not believe in it.
By grasping at the meaning according to its superficial characteristics, they will suffer calamities throughout kalpas.
These bhikṣus likewise claim for themselves: "I am a Dharma-master," "I am a Vinaya-master," and "I am a Meditation-master."
These three types of practitioners can extinguish my Dharma,
and no others. These three types of people will, moreover, mutually criticize one another's faults.
Mutually reviling one another—
these three kinds of people enter hell as if struck by an arrow.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Nityadāna addressed the Buddha,
saying, "World-Honored One, when will these bhikṣus emerge?
The Buddha replied, "Good son, one thousand years after my parinirvāṇa."
Unwholesome dharmas will gradually arise;
one thousand and one hundred years hence,
wicked bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs will be found throughout Jambudvīpa.
They are filled everywhere;
they do not cultivate the Way or its virtue,
but seek wealth and property excessively, practicing only what is unlawful.
He kept many kinds of the eight types of impure things;
his person lacked the ten virtues, yet he kept two śrāmaṇeras.
Before his *varṣa* count had reached ten, he already ordained śrāmaṇeras.
Because of these causes and conditions, all laypeople came to despise the Triple Gem.
From that time forward, both monastics and laypeople vied with one another to construct stūpas and temples until they filled the world.
Stupas, temples, and images are found everywhere;
they may be located in mountains, forests, or wildernesses,
or by the side of roads.
Or perhaps they are located on streets and in foul, filthy, and wretched places—
ruinous, dilapidated, and neglected by anyone. At such times,
although monastics and laypeople may construct stupas and temples to make offerings to the Triple Gem, [the existing ones remain in decay].
Furthermore, they do not give rise to reverence for the Triple Gem;
when inviting the Sangha to the monastery, they do not provide them with food, drink, clothing, bedding, or medicinal requisites,
but instead go so far as to borrow and beg from them.
Consuming the food of the Sangha, they do not fear the sufferings of the three miserable realms in the future.
At that time, all laypeople, regardless of their social rank,
will exclusively seek to bring harm to the Sangha, encroaching upon, damaging, and disturbing them.
They do not wish to provide protection.
Such people as these will fall forever into the three miserable realms.
O son of good family!
In future ages, all secular officials will have no faith in the retribution of sin and merit;
they will tax and seize the property of the Sangha,
or levy taxes on the grain and rice of livestock, even down to an object as small as a single hair.
Whether they are servants of the Triple Gem or oxen and horses belonging to the Triple Gem,
no secular official shall beat or strike such servants or animals.
They shall not even accept prostrations from the slaves of the Triple Gem;
all such acts incur calamity and retribution.
How much more so, then, to drive them, whip them, or beat them?
He addressed the secular officials:
"In any place where there is a prohibition against crossing or where taxes are collected,
take care not to let bhikṣus pay such taxes."
If one wishes to tax those who have left the household life, they will incur immeasurable sin.
Good son, at that time,
if all monastics and laypeople perform meritorious deeds, [they shall be protected].
One should practice giving to those who are orphaned, aged, impoverished, or afflicted by malignant diseases. Furthermore,
one should repair ruined stūpas and temples, as well as various sacred images,
regardless of whether the work is permitted by oneself or by others.
According to their respective capacities, all [ailments] are healed.
The merit of such a person is inconceivable;
for by merely practicing [this], there is no need to create anything new.
Good son, why is it that in future ages all laypeople will despise the Triple Gem?
It is precisely because the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs do not act in accordance with the Dharma.
Though they wear the dharma robes upon their bodies, they lightly attend to worldly affairs;
some support themselves by selling goods in markets,
while others travel on roads as merchants seeking profit.
Some engage in the craft of painting or other artistic skills;
some practice divination regarding the various fortunes and misfortunes of men and women;
and others drink wine to the point of intoxication, engaging in singing, dancing, and musical entertainment.
Some play at go or six-man chess;
some bhikṣus employ deceitful speech when teaching the Dharma in order to seek the favor of others;
or they recite incantations and arts to treat the illnesses of others.
Or again, though practicing dhyāna, they are unable to attain single-minded concentration;
instead, they use the methods of false meditative absorption to divinate good and bad fortune,
or they practice acupuncture and various medicinal decoctions in order to seek food and clothing.
For this reason, it causes ordinary worldly people to fail to give rise to respect,
except for Bodhisattvas who act for the benefit of sentient beings.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva Constantly Giving.
"Good son, in future ages, among both monastics and laypeople,
there will be various evil persons who create and erect images of me or images of bodhisattvas."
They sell [relics] for profit to sustain themselves;
neither monastics nor laypeople recognize the distinction between sin and merit,
purchasing them to offer as worship.
Both incur offense.
For five hundred lifetimes, they shall constantly be sold by others. Good son!
In future ages, all sentient beings who fashion images shall not fully accomplish all the marks;
some may even create only half-bodies.
Some have hands and feet that are not formed;
their ears, noses, eyes, and mouths are all incomplete,
being merely coarse shadows and echoes.
Or they may construct stupas and temples but fail to install images;
or if there are ruined stupas or damaged images, they do not repair them.
Such people shall incur immeasurable transgressions.
"Good son,
in future ages, various bhikṣus will,
within their respective places of residence, collectively proclaim and establish regulations."
To prevent [the accumulation of food], the Sangha of the four directions may collectively establish a limit for eating,
whether for one day or ten days,
or for five, four, three, or two days, even down to a single meal.
These bhikṣus, at the end of their lives, will fall into the hells, among hungry ghosts, or as animals, where they will suffer endlessly.
Furthermore, there may be bhikṣus or śrāmaṇeras who treat the property of the Saṃgha as if it were their own personal possession.
One may take and use it as one pleases,
eat it at improper times,
or give it to friends and relatives.
These bhikṣus and śrāmaṇeras shall never again hear the Dharma,
even until the appearance of a thousand Buddhas in the world;
they shall forever remain within the three miserable realms, where there is no place for repentance.
If one dwells together with such a person,
all ritual acts performed, such as the *karmavācanā* and the *poṣadha*, will fail to be accomplished;
all shall incur transgressions.
"Good son, if there are those who have committed the four grave offenses or the five heinous crimes,
they can easily be saved through repentance."
If one appropriates even a single hair or a single grain of the Sangha's property,
eats at improper times,
or takes and gives things according to one's own will;
They will sink forever into the ocean of suffering with no time of escape;
or they will encounter various misfortunes and afflictions in this present life.
If one dwells together with such a person, [the same consequences will follow].
Day and night they commit offenses. Good son,
in future ages there will be various laypeople who do not recognize the nature of sin and merit.
If one sells images of the Buddha, scriptures, banners, or flowers created by one’s own grandfather or by oneself to others in order to support one's wife and children,
such items should not be purchased either.
At that time, all secular officials who possess authority should seize this person,
subject him to severe flogging and punishment, and drive him out of the country. Good son!
In future ages, there will be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, as well as kings, ministers, palace ladies, and queens,
who violate the prohibitive precepts, lacking a sense of shame and remorse, and failing to perform repentance.
By these causes and conditions, they cause the Dharma to become defiled and turbid. Good son,
in future ages there will be many evil bhikṣus.
They cling to their dwelling places like worldly people,
guarding their own houses and unable to move them once every three months according to the proper time.
They saw a bhikṣu who, carrying his own robes and bowl, remained at his dwelling for a full ninety days and then moved on.
All those wicked bhikṣus spoke as follows:
This bhikṣu is of unsettled disposition;
he is restless, burdened with many affairs, deranged and lost of mind,
and frequently shifts his position.
One who speaks such words shall incur immeasurable guilt.
Good son, in the future age when various evils arise, [this shall come to pass].
All monastics and laypeople alike should practice great loving-kindness and great compassion.
When enduring the provocations of others, they should reflect:
"All sentient beings have been my parents since beginningless time."
All sentient beings, from time immemorial, have all been my brothers, sisters, wives, children, and kinsmen.
For this reason,
one should regard all sentient beings with compassion and pity, providing relief according to one's ability.
If one sees sentient beings suffering from hardship and distress, and employs various skillful means— disregarding even one's own body and life—
at that time, whether it be a king, a high minister, or the ruler of a city, town, or village.
If there are powerful householders, brahmins, and so forth,
as well as influential bhikṣus,
they should exhort these people not to turn back.
Support their power so that wicked people do not create obstacles for them,
and do not allow wicked people to plunder their wealth.
To assist them in this way—
The merit of that person cannot be fully described.
At that time, with a heart of compassion, they practiced giving to the poor, the orphaned, the elderly, and all those in distress, even down to the smallest ants.
Its merit is most supreme.
Good son, if I were to explain at length the merit of giving to those who are destitute, impoverished, or afflicted by illness, [it would be vast].
It would not be exhausted even at the end of an eon;
now that the time for Nirvana has arrived,
I shall explain it briefly for you.
At that time, when the entire great assembly heard the Buddha speak of the various calamities and transformations during the period of the Semblance Dharma in future ages,
the hair on their bodies stood on end, and they wailed and wept with grief, unable to restrain themselves.
The Buddha addressed the great assembly:
"Cease, do not weep;
such is the natural law of the world."
"Goodness must be followed by evil;
prosperity must be followed by decline.
The Buddha further addressed the Bodhisattva Constantly Giving:
"Set aside this matter for now.
By what marks do you perceive the Tathāgata?
And by what marks do you perceive sentient beings?"
The Bodhisattva Constantly Bestowing said to the Buddha,
"World-Honored One, I observe that the Tathāgata does not originate from a prior limit."
Not reaching the other shore,
not dwelling in the middle,
neither existent nor non-existent.
It neither emerges nor subsides;
it is neither form nor non-form;
it is neither conditioned nor unconditioned.
It is neither eternal nor annihilated;
it is neither with outflows nor without outflows;
it is equal to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), like empty space.
From his initial attainment of enlightenment until his parinirvāṇa,
throughout that interval, no single word of Dharma was ever seen by anyone to have been spoken by the Tathāgata.
Yet, all sentient beings perceive him appearing and disappearing, preaching the Dharma, and delivering living beings.
The realm of the Tathāgata is inconceivable;
it cannot be cognized by consciousness,
nor can it be known by wisdom.
It transcends the three periods of time yet is not separate from the three periods of time;
only the Tathāgata has personally awakened to this Dharma.
As I contemplate the Tathāgata, he is indeed such as this.
World-Honored One, as I now contemplate the characteristics of the four great elements of all sentient beings,
they are like clouds in the sky and like a mirage in the heat.
Like a city of Gandharvas,
like an illusion, like a magical transformation,
like an empty village.
Like an image in a mirror,
like the moon in water,
like an echo in a valley.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are all likewise so.
World-Honored One, the characteristics of the minds of sentient beings are inconceivable;
they cannot be known by śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattvas of the lower stages.
World-Honored One, the characteristics of sentient beings neither come nor go;
they are neither existent nor non-existent.
Neither internal nor external;
when coming, there is nowhere from which it comes;
when going, there is nowhere to which it goes.
Yet they constantly transmigrate and undergo suffering in vain;
this is all because sentient beings have, since time immemorial, been deeply attached to the view of a self.
Because of attachment to a self, craving increases;
through the law of the twelve links of dependent origination,
one suffers for a long night without end.
The characteristics of sentient beings are originally empty and quiescent.
For this reason, the Bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion within them.
World-Honored One, all the wholesome and unwholesome karmas of sentient beings are produced solely by the one mind.
There is no other dharma;
such, I observe, are the characteristics of sentient beings.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Constantly Bestowing.
Excellent, excellent!
It is well that you have expounded this Dharma.
What you have now spoken is also approved by the Buddha.
When a bodhisattva practices the four means of attraction and the six perfections,
they should contemplate the characteristics of sentient beings in this manner. Good son!
When a bodhisattva practices giving,
they do not discriminate between fields of merit and non-fields of merit; rather,
upon seeing any being in poverty or suffering, they bestow gifts upon them all.
When practicing generosity, one should maintain this contemplation:
not perceiving the recipient,
nor perceiving the giver.
Material wealth is likewise so.
These three things are all empty, equal, and without attachment. Why is this?
When practicing generosity while realizing that all phenomena are devoid of self and what belongs to a self,
one does not hope for rewards in the present,
nor does one hope for the pleasures of humans or devas in the future.
He practices giving solely for the sake of seeking great enlightenment for all sentient beings;
he practices giving out of a desire to bring peace and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings;
and he practices giving out of a desire to gather in those sentient beings who are evil and establish them in wholesome dharmas.
Again, he makes this contemplation:
the characteristics of the realm of bodhi and the characteristics of the realm of sentient beings are both empty and quiescent.
It is by relying on words and letters that one delivers sentient beings and attains bodhi.
Within the true Dharma, there is neither attainment nor realization. Good son!
It is like a person who, in a night dream, sees various things;
perhaps they dream that they themselves are imprisoned and bound by officials, undergoing various sufferings,
giving rise to great distress and affliction before finally being released.
Shortly thereafter, he again dreamed that he was a great king,
possessing sovereign power and majesty and enjoying great happiness.
While in the dream, he had this thought:
"I was suffering in such a manner at last night's hour;
now, once again, I freely experience great bliss.
Having formed this thought, he suddenly awoke from sleep.
One knows not where matters of suffering and pleasure reside.
Such dream-phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent;
all dharmas are likewise so.
"One who practices this contemplation is said to practice correctly.
When this Dharma was spoken,
immeasurable bodhisattvas attained the rank of Buddhahood.
Innumerable bodhisattvas attained the stage of being born only once more before Buddhahood.
Innumerable bodhisattvas each achieved further advancement according to their respective practices.
Innumerable humans and devas attained the fruits of the four paths.
Immeasurable śrāvakas entered the stage of bodhisattvas;
immeasurable beings of various kinds gave rise to the aspiration for enlightenment. Good son!
In future ages, if the fourfold assembly of disciples hears this sutra and gives rise to a heart of joy,
the merit they shall obtain will be immeasurable and boundless.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda and the great multitude:
"You should receive and uphold this well, and be careful not to forget or lose it.
This sutra is titled 'Resolving Doubts during the Semblance Dharma';
it is also titled 'Saving the Orphans and Solitary'."
Thus it was received and upheld.
At that time, the great assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken,
received it with single-minded reverence, paid their respects, and departed.
Together they prepared the implements for cremation, their grief moving heaven and earth.
*The Sūtra on Resolving Doubts Concerning the Semblance Dharma* ends.
